{{Short description|Matrix decomposition}}

The '''compact representation''' for [[quasi-Newton methods]] is a [[matrix decomposition]], which is typically used in [[gradient]] based [[optimization (mathematics)|optimization]] [[algorithms]] or for solving [[nonlinear systems]]. The decomposition uses a low-rank representation for the direct and/or inverse [[Hessian matrix|Hessian]] or the [[Jacobian matrix and determinant|Jacobian]] of a nonlinear system. Because of this, the compact representation is often used for large problems and [[constrained optimization]].

[[File:Main-figure0.pdf|thumb|upright=1.75|alt=The compact matrix decomposition of a dense Hessian approximation|The compact representation (right) of a dense Hessian approximation (left) is an initial matrix (typically diagonal) plus low rank decomposition. It has a small memory footprint (shaded areas) and enables efficient matrix computations]]

== Definition ==
The compact representation of a quasi-Newton matrix for the inverse Hessian <math>H_k</math> or
direct Hessian <math>B_k</math> of a nonlinear [[loss function|objective function]] 
<math>f(x):\mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R} </math> expresses a sequence of recursive rank-1
or rank-2 matrix updates as one rank-<math>k</math> or rank-<math>2k</math> update of an initial matrix.<ref name="nw">{{cite book |last1=Nocedal|first1= J.|last2=Wright|first2=S.J.|date=2006 |title= Numerical Optimization |series= Springer Series in Operations Research and Financial Engineering|url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-0-387-40065-5|publisher=Springer New York, NY |doi= 10.1007/978-0-387-40065-5|isbn= 978-0-387-30303-1}}</ref><ref name="compthes">{{cite thesis |last=Brust |first=J. J. |date=2018 |title=Large-Scale Quasi-Newton Trust-Region Methods: High-Accuracy Solvers, Dense Initializations, and Extensions |url=https://escholarship.org/uc/item/2bv922qk |degree=PhD |publisher=University of California, Merced}}</ref>
Because it is derived from quasi-Newton updates,
it uses differences of iterates and gradients <math>\nabla f(x_k) = g_k </math> in its definition
<math> \{s_{i-1}=x_{i}-x_{i-1},y_{i-1}=g_{i}-g_{i-1} \}_{i=1}^k </math>.
In particular, for <math>r=k </math> or <math> r=2k </math> the rectangular <math> n \times r </math> matrices <math> U_k, J_k </math>  and the <math> r \times r </math> square symmetric systems <math> M_k, N_k </math> depend on the <math>s_i,y_i</math>'s and define the quasi-Newton representations

:<math> H_k = H_0 + U_k M^{-1}_k U^T_k, \quad \text{ and } \quad B_k = B_0 + J_k N^{-1}_k J^T_k </math>   
<!-- :<math> B_k = B_0 + J_k N^{-1}_k J^T_k </math> -->

=== Applications ===
Because of the special matrix decomposition the compact representation is implemented in 
state-of-the-art optimization software.<ref name="knitro">{{cite book |last1=Byrd|first1= R. H.|last2=Nocedal|first2=J|last3=Waltz|first3=R. A.|title= Large-Scale Nonlinear Optimization|date=2006 |chapter= KNITRO: An integrated package for nonlinear optimization |series= Nonconvex Optimization and Its Applications|volume= 83|chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.1007/0-387-30065-1_4|location=In: Di Pillo, G., Roma, M. (eds) Large-Scale Nonlinear Optimization. Nonconvex Optimization and Its Applications, vol 83. |publisher=Springer, Boston, MA. |pages=35–59|doi= 10.1007/0-387-30065-1_4|isbn= 978-0-387-30063-4}}</ref><ref name="lbfgsb">{{cite journal|doi=10.1145/279232.279236|last1=Zhu|first1= C.|last2=Byrd|first2= R. H.|last3=Lu|first3= P.| last4=Nocedal|first4= J.|title=Algorithm 778: L-BFGS-B: Fortran subroutines for large-scale bound-constrained optimization|year=1997|journal= ACM Transactions on Mathematical Software |volume=23|issue= 4|pages=550–560}}</ref><ref name="scsr1">{{cite journal|doi=10.1145/3550269|last1=Brust|first1= J.|last2=Burdakov|first2= O.|last3=Erway|first3= J.| last4=Marcia|first4= R.|title=Algorithm 1030: SC-SR1: MATLAB software for limited-memory SR1 trust-region methods|year=2022|journal= ACM Transactions on Mathematical Software |volume=48|issue= 4|pages=1–33}}</ref><ref name="ipopt">
{{cite journal|doi=10.1007/s10107-004-0559-y|last1=Wächter|first1= A.|last2=Biegler|first2= L. T.|title=On the implementation of an interior-point filter line-search algorithm for large-scale nonlinear programming|year=2006|journal= Mathematical Programming|volume=106|pages=25–57}}</ref>
When combined with limited-memory techniques it is a popular technique for [[constrained optimization]] with gradients.<ref name="compact">{{cite journal|doi=10.1007/BF01582063|last1=Byrd|first1= R. H.|last2= Nocedal|first2=J.|last3= Schnabel|first3= R. B.|title=Representations of Quasi-Newton Matrices and their use in Limited Memory Methods|year=1994|journal= Mathematical Programming|volume=63|issue= 4|pages=129–156|s2cid=5581219}}</ref> 
[[Linear algebra]] operations can be done efficiently, like [[Matrix multiplication|matrix-vector products]], [[Gaussian elimination|solves]] or [[Eigendecomposition of a matrix|eigendecompositions]]. It can be combined
with [[line-search]] and [[trust region]] techniques, and the representation has been developed for many quasi-Newton
updates. For instance, the matrix vector product with the direct quasi-Newton Hessian and an arbitrary
vector <math>g \in \mathbb{R}^n </math> is:
:<math>
\begin{align}
p^{(0)}_k &= J^T_k g \\
\text{solve} \quad N_k p^{(1)}_k &= p^{(0)}_k \quad \quad \text{(}N_k \text{ is small)} \\
p^{(2)}_k &= J_k p^{(1)}_k \\
p^{(3)}_k &= H_0 g \\
p^{\phantom{(4)}}_k       &= p^{(2)}_k + p^{(3)}_k
\end{align}
</math>

=== Background ===
In the context of the [[Generalized minimal residual method|GMRES]] method, Walker<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1137/0909010|last=Walker|first= H. F.|title=Implementation of the GMRES Method Using Householder Transformations|year=1988|journal= SIAM Journal on Scientific and Statistical Computing|volume=9|issue= 1|pages=152–163 }}</ref>
showed that a product of [[Householder transformation]]s (an identity plus rank-1) can be expressed as 
a compact matrix formula. This led to the derivation
<!-- <ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1007/BF01582063|last1=Byrd|first1= R. H.|last2= Nocedal|first2=J.|last3= Schnabel|first3= R. B.|title=Representations of Quasi-Newton Matrices and their use in Limited Memory Methods|year=1994|journal= Mathematical Programming|volume=63|issue= 4|pages=129–156|s2cid=5581219}}</ref> -->
of an explicit matrix expression for the product of <math>k</math> identity plus rank-1 matrices.<ref name="compact" />
Specifically, for 
<math display="inline"> S_k = \begin{bmatrix} s_0 & s_1 & \ldots s_{k-1} \end{bmatrix},</math>
<math>~Y_k = \begin{bmatrix} y_0 & y_1 & \ldots y_{k-1} \end{bmatrix}, </math>
<math>~(R_k)_{ij} = s^T_{i-1} y_{j-1},  </math>
<math>~\rho_{i-1} = 1/s^T_{i-1} y_{i-1} </math> and
<math display="inline">~V_i = I - \rho_{i-1} y_{i-1} s^T_{i-1}</math> when
<math> 1 \le i \le j \le k </math>
the product of <math>k</math> rank-1 updates to the identity is
<math display="block"> \prod_{i=1}^k V_{i-1} = 
\left( I - \rho_{0} y_{0} s^T_{0} \right) \cdots \left( I - \rho_{k-1} y_{k-1} s^T_{k-1} \right)
= I - Y_k R^{-1}_k S^T_k </math>
The [[BFGS]] update can be expressed in terms of products of the <math>V_i </math>'s, which 
have a compact matrix formula. Therefore, the BFGS recursion can exploit these [[block matrix]]
representations

{{NumBlk|:| <math display="block">
\begin{align}
H_k &=  V_{k-1} H_{k-1} V^T_{k-1} + \rho_{k-1} s_{k-1} s^T_{k-1} \\
    &=  \left( V_{k-1} \cdots V_1 V_0) H_0 (V^T_0 V^T_1 \cdots V^T_{k-1} \right) + \\
    &\phantom{=}  \rho_0 \left( V_{k-1} \cdots V_1 \right)  s_0 s^T_0 \left( V^T_1 \cdots V^T_{k-1} \right) + \\
    &\phantom{=}  \quad \vdots  \\
    &\phantom{=} \rho_{k-2} V_{k-1} s_{k-2} s^T_{k-2} V^T_{k-1} + \\
    &\phantom{=} \rho_{k-1} s_{k-1} s^T_{k-1}
\end{align}
</math>|{{EquationRef|1}}}}

== Recursive quasi-Newton updates ==
A [[parametric family]] of quasi-Newton updates includes many of the most known formulas.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1137/1019005|last1=Dennis|first1= Jr, J. E.|last2=Moré|first2= J. J.|title=Quasi-Newton methods, motivation and theory|year=1977|journal= SIAM Review|volume=19|issue= 1|pages=46–89|hdl=1813/6056 |url=https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-01495720/file/DMQO.pdf |hdl-access=free}}</ref> For
arbitrary vectors <math>v_{k}</math> and <math>c_{k}</math> such that <math>v^T_{k}y_{k}\ne 0</math> and 
<math>c^T_{k}s_{k} \ne 0 </math> general recursive update formulas for the inverse and direct Hessian
estimates are
{{NumBlk|:|
<math display="block">
 H_{k+1} = H_{k} + \frac{(s_{k} - H_{k}y_{k} )v^T_{k} + v_{k}(s_{k} - H_{k}y_{k})^T }{v^T_{k} y_{k}}
- \frac{(s_{k}-H_{k}y_{k})^T y_{k}}{(v^T_{k} y_{k})^2} v_{k} v^T_{k}
</math>|{{EquationRef|2}}}}
{{NumBlk|:|
<math display="block">
 B_{k+1} = B_{k} + \frac{(y_{k} - B_{k}s_{k} )c^T_{k} + c_{k}(y_{k} - B_{k}s_{k})^T }{c^T_{k} s_{k}}
- \frac{(y_{k}-B_{k}s_{k})^T s_{k}}{(c^T_{k} s_{k})^2} c_{k} c^T_{k}
</math>|{{EquationRef|3}}}}

By making specific choices for the parameter vectors <math>v_{k}</math> and <math>c_{k}</math> well known
methods are recovered

{| class="wikitable"
|+ Table 1: Quasi-Newton updates parametrized by vectors <math>v_{k}</math> and <math>c_{k}</math>
|-
! <math>v_{k}</math> !! <math>\text{method}</math> !! <math>c_{k}</math> !! <math>\text{method}</math> 
|-
|<math> s_{k} </math> || 	[[BFGS]] || 	<math> s_{k} </math> || 	PSB (Powell Symmetric Broyden)
|-
|<math> y_{k} </math> || 	<math> \text{Greenstadt's} </math> || 	<math> y_{k} </math> || 	[[Davidon–Fletcher–Powell formula|DFP]] 
|-
|<math> s_{k}-H_{k}y_{k} </math> || 	[[Symmetric rank-one|SR1]] || 	<math> y_{k}-B_{k}s_{k} </math> || 	[[Symmetric rank-one|SR1]]
|- 
| || || <math>P_k^{\text{S}} s_k </math><ref><math>S_{k+1} =  
\begin{bmatrix}
s_0 & \ldots & s_{k}
\end{bmatrix},~P_k^{\text{S}}=I-S_{k+1}(S_{k+1}^T S_{k+1})^{-1} S_{k+1}^T</math>
</ref>
|| MSS (Multipoint-Symmetric-Secant)
|}

<!-- <math>S_{k+1} =  
\begin{bmatrix}
s_0 & \ldots & s_{k}
\end{bmatrix},
P_k^{\text{S}} = I - S_{k+1}(S_{k+1}^T S_{k+1})^{-1}S_{k+1}^T  </math> -->

== Compact Representations ==
<!-- Since many quasi-Newton methods follow from the general updates in ({{EquationNote|2}}) and ({{EquationNote|3}})
the compact representation of these updates consequently give the representation of most QN formulas. -->

Collecting the updating vectors of the recursive formulas into matrices, define

<math display="block"> S_k = \begin{bmatrix} s_0 & s_1 & \ldots & s_{k-1} \end{bmatrix}, </math>
<math display="block"> Y_k = \begin{bmatrix} y_0 & y_1 & \ldots & y_{k-1} \end{bmatrix}, </math>
<math display="block"> V_k = \begin{bmatrix} v_0 & v_1 & \ldots & v_{k-1} \end{bmatrix}, </math>
<math display="block"> C_k = \begin{bmatrix} c_0 & c_1 & \ldots & c_{k-1} \end{bmatrix}, </math>

upper triangular

<math display="block"> \big(R_k\big)_{ij} := \big(R^{\text{SY}}_k\big)_{ij} = s^T_{i-1}y_{j-1}, \quad  \big(R^{\text{VY}}_k\big)_{ij} = v^T_{i-1}y_{j-1}
, \quad  \big(R^{\text{CS}}_k\big)_{ij} = c^T_{i-1}s_{j-1}, \quad \quad \text{ for } 1 \le i \le j \le k  </math>

lower triangular

<math display="block" > \big(L_k\big)_{ij} := \big(L^{\text{SY}}_k\big)_{ij} = s^T_{i-1}y_{j-1}, \quad  \big(L^{\text{VY}}_k\big)_{ij} = v^T_{i-1}y_{j-1}
, \quad  \big(L^{\text{CS}}_k\big)_{ij} = c^T_{i-1}s_{j-1}, \quad \quad \text{ for } 1 \le j < i \le k  </math>

and diagonal

<math display="block" > (D_k)_{ij} := \big(D^{\text{SY}}_k\big)_{ij} = s^T_{i-1}y_{j-1}, \quad \quad \text{ for } 1 \le i = j \le k </math>

With these definitions the compact representations of general rank-2 updates in ({{EquationNote|2}}) and ({{EquationNote|3}})  (including the well known quasi-Newton updates in Table 1) 
<!-- are
given by for each formula:
the general rank-2 updates -->
have been developed in Brust:<ref name="brust24">{{cite arXiv |eprint=2403.12206 |class=math.OC |first1=J. J. |last1=Brust |title=Useful Compact Representations for Data-Fitting |year=2024}}</ref> 
<!-- The formula for the inverse update 
is <ref name="msscompact" /> -->

{{NumBlk|:|
<math display="block"> H_k = H_0 + U_k M^{-1}_k U^T_k, </math>
|{{EquationRef|4}}}}

<math display="block"> U_k = \begin{bmatrix} V_k & S_k - H_0 Y_k \end{bmatrix} </math>

<math display="block"> M_k = 
\begin{bmatrix} 0_{k \times k} & R^{\text{VY}}_k \\ 
\big( R^{\text{VY}}_k \big)^T & R_k+R^T_k-(D_k+Y^T_k H_0 Y_k) 
\end{bmatrix} </math>

and the formula for the direct Hessian is

{{NumBlk|:|
<math display="block"> B_k = B_0 + J_k N^{-1}_k J^T_k, </math>
|{{EquationRef|5}}}}

<math display="block"> J_k = \begin{bmatrix} C_k & Y_k - B_0 S_k \end{bmatrix} </math>

<math display="block"> N_k = 
\begin{bmatrix} 0_{k \times k} & R^{\text{CS}}_k \\ 
\big( R^{\text{CS}}_k \big)^T & R_k+R^T_k-(D_k+S^T_k B_0 S_k) 
\end{bmatrix} </math>

For instance, when <math>V_k = S_k</math> the representation in ({{EquationNote|4}}) is
the compact formula for the BFGS recursion in ({{EquationNote|1}}). <!-- The validity of these expressions
can be simply checked by numerically comparing the difference between, e.g., ({{EquationNote|2}}) and
({{EquationNote|4}}) (or, ({{EquationNote|3}}) and
({{EquationNote|5}})) for the same <math>k</math>. -->
<!-- 
=== Specific Representations ===
Without the parametrized update, (eqs. ({{EquationNote|2}}), ({{EquationNote|3}})), which represents many well known formulas, the compact representation is specific to each quasi-Newton recursion. However, all formulas are expressed as an initial matrix plus a low rank update, and are equivalent to (eqs. ({{EquationNote|2}}) or ({{EquationNote|3}})) whenever there is an equivalence in the recursive formulas of the updates. -->
<!-- -->
<!-- === Representations without general recurrences (eqs. ({{EquationNote|2}}), ({{EquationNote|3}})) ===
Prior to the development of the compact representations of ({{EquationNote|2}}) and ({{EquationNote|3}}),
equivalent representations have been discovered for most known updates (see Table 1). -->
=== Specific Representations ===
Prior to the development of the compact representations of ({{EquationNote|2}}) and ({{EquationNote|3}}),
equivalent representations have been discovered for most known updates (see Table 1).

==== [[Broyden–Fletcher–Goldfarb–Shanno algorithm|BFGS]] ====
<!-- An equivalent compact representation for the BFGS (Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno) exists<ref name="compact" />. -->
Along with the SR1 representation, the BFGS (Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno) compact representation was the first compact formula known.<ref name="compact" /> In particular, the inverse representation is 
given by

<math> H_k = H_0 + U_k M^{-1}_k U^T_k, \quad U_k = \begin{bmatrix} S_k & H_0 Y_k \end{bmatrix}, \quad  M^{-1}_k =
\left[\begin{smallmatrix} R^{-T}_k(D_k+Y^T_k H_0 Y_k) R^{-1}_k & -R^{-T}_k \\ -R^{-1}_k & 0 \end{smallmatrix} \right]</math> 
<!-- After simplification, this formula is exactly ({{EquationNote|4}}) with <math>V_k = S_k </math>. -->
The direct Hessian approximation can be found by applying the [[Woodbury matrix identity|Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury identity]] to the inverse Hessian:

<math> B_k = B_0 + J_k N^{-1}_k J^T_k, \quad J_k = \begin{bmatrix} B_0 S_k & Y_k \end{bmatrix}, \quad  N_k =
\left[\begin{smallmatrix} S^T B_0 S_k & L_k \\ L^T_k & -D_k \end{smallmatrix} \right]</math>

==== [[Symmetric rank-one|SR1]] ====
The SR1 (Symmetric Rank-1) compact representation was first proposed in.<ref name="compact" /> Using the definitions of
<math>D_k, L_k </math> and <math>R_k </math> from above, the inverse Hessian formula is given by

<math> H_k = H_0 + U_k M^{-1}_k U^T_k, \quad U_k = S_k-H_0 Y_k, \quad  M_k =
R_k+R^T_k-D_k-Y^T_k H_0 Y_k </math>

The direct Hessian is obtained by the Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury identity and has the form

<math> B_k = B_0 + J_k N^{-1}_k J^T_k, \quad J_k = Y_k-B_0 S_k, \quad  N_k =
D_k+L_k+L^T_k-S^T_k B_0 S_k </math>

==== MSS ==== 
The multipoint symmetric secant (MSS) method is a method that aims to satisfy multiple secant equations. The recursive
update formula was originally developed by Burdakov.<ref name="mssoriginal">{{cite journal|doi=10.1080/01630568308816160|last1=Burdakov|first1= O. P.|title=Methods of the secant type for systems of equations with symmetric Jacobian matrix|year=1983|journal= Numerical Functional Analysis and Optimization|volume=6|issue=2|pages=1–18}}</ref> The compact representation for the direct Hessian was derived in <ref name="msscompact">{{cite journal|doi=10.1023/A:1021561204463|last1=Burdakov|first1= O. P.|last2= Martínez|first2=J. M. |last3= Pilotta|first3= E. A.|title=A limited-memory multipoint symmetric secant method for bound constrained optimization|year=2002|journal= Annals of Operations Research |volume=117|issue=1–4 |pages=51–70 |url=http://urn.kb.se/resolve?urn=urn:nbn:se:liu:diva-48712 }}</ref><!-- <ref name="compthes" /> -->

<math> B_k = B_0 + J_k N^{-1}_k J^T_k, \quad J_k = \begin{bmatrix} S_k & Y_k - B_0 S_k \end{bmatrix}, \quad  N_k =
\left[\begin{smallmatrix} W_k(S^T_k B_0 S_k - (R_k - D_k +R^T_k))W_k & W_k \\ W_k & 0 \end{smallmatrix} \right]^{-1}, \quad W_k = (S^T_k S_k)^{-1} </math>

Another equivalent compact representation for the MSS matrix is derived by rewriting <math>J_k </math> 
in terms of <math>J_k = \begin{bmatrix} S_k & B_0 Y_k \end{bmatrix}</math>.<ref name="scmss">{{cite journal|doi=10.1080/10556788.2023.2296441|last1=Brust|first1= J. J.|last2= Erway|first2=J. B. |last3= Marcia|first3= R. F.|title=Shape-changing trust-region methods using multipoint symmetric secant matrices|year=2024|journal= Optimization Methods and Software |volume=39 |issue=5 |pages=990–1007|arxiv=2209.12057 }}</ref>
The inverse representation can be obtained by application for the Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury identity.

==== [[Davidon–Fletcher–Powell formula|DFP]] ====
Since the DFP (Davidon Fletcher Powell) update is the dual of the BFGS formula (i.e., swapping <math> H_k \leftrightarrow B_k </math>, <math> H_0 \leftrightarrow B_0 </math> and <math> y_k \leftrightarrow s_k </math> in the BFGS update), the compact representation for DFP can be immediately obtained from the one for BFGS.<ref>{{cite conference |last1=Erway |first1=J. B. |last2=Jain |first2=V. | last3=Marcia | first3=R. F.| title=Shifted limited-memory DFP systems |year=2013 |conference=In 2013 Asilomar Conference on Signals, Systems and Computers |publisher=IEEE|pages=1033–1037 }}</ref>

==== PSB ====
The PSB (Powell-Symmetric-Broyden) compact representation was developed for the direct Hessian approximation.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1007/s12532-023-00238-4|last1=Kanzow|first1= C. |last2= Steck|first2=D. |title=Regularization of limited memory quasi-Newton methods for large-scale nonconvex minimization|year=2023|journal= Mathematical Programming Computation|volume=15|issue=3|pages=417–444|doi-access=free|arxiv=1911.04584}}</ref> It is equivalent to substituting <math> C_k = S_k </math> in ({{EquationNote|5}})

<math> B_k = B_0 + J_k N^{-1}_k J^T_k, \quad J_k = \begin{bmatrix} S_k & Y_k-B_0 S_k \end{bmatrix}, \quad  
N_k =
\left[\begin{smallmatrix} 0 & R^{\text{SS}}_k \\ (R^{\text{SS}}_k)^T & R_k+R^T_k-(D_k + S^T_k B_0 S_k) \end{smallmatrix} \right]
</math>

==== Structured BFGS ====
For structured optimization problems in which the objective function can be decomposed into two parts
<math>f(x) = \widehat{k}(x) + \widehat{u}(x) </math>, where the gradients and Hessian of <math>\widehat{k}(x) </math>
are known but only the gradient of <math> \widehat{u}(x) </math> is known, structured BFGS formulas
exist. The compact representation of these methods has the general form of ({{EquationNote|5}}),
with specific <math>J_k</math> and <math>N_k</math>.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1007/s10589-021-00297-0|last1=Brust|first1= J. J |last2= Di|first2=Z.|last3=Leyffer|first3=S.|last4=Petra|first4=C. G. |title=Compact representations of structured BFGS matrices|year=2021|journal= Computational Optimization and Applications|volume=80|issue=1|pages=55–88|arxiv=2208.00057 }}</ref>

==== Reduced BFGS ====
The reduced compact representation (RCR) of BFGS is for linear equality constrained optimization
<math> \text{ minimize } f(x) \text{ subject to: } Ax = b </math>, where <math>A</math> is [[Underdetermined system|underdetermined]]. In addition to the matrices
<math>S_k, Y_k </math> the RCR also stores the projections of the <math>y_i</math>'s onto the nullspace of <math>A</math>

<math display="block> Z_k = \begin{bmatrix} z_0 & z_1 & \cdots z_{k-1} \end{bmatrix}, \quad z_i = P y_i, 
\quad P = I - A (A^TA)^{-1} A^T, \quad 0 \le i \le k-1 </math>

For <math>B_k</math> the compact representation of the BFGS matrix (with a multiple of the identity <math>B_0</math>) the (1,1) block of the inverse [[Karush–Kuhn–Tucker conditions|KKT]] matrix has the compact representation<ref name="rcr">{{cite journal|doi=10.1137/21M1393819|last1=Brust|first1= J. J |last2= Marcia|first2=R.F.|last3=Petra|first3=C.G.|last4=Saunders|first4=M. A. |title=Large-scale optimization with linear equality constraints using reduced compact representation|year=2022|journal= SIAM Journal on Scientific Computing|volume=44|issue=1|pages=A103–A127|arxiv=2101.11048 |bibcode=2022SJSC...44A.103B }}</ref>

<math>
K_k =
\begin{bmatrix}
B_k & A^T \\
A & 0
\end{bmatrix},
\quad B_0 =  \frac{1}{\gamma_k}I, \quad H_0 =  \gamma_k I, \quad \gamma_k > 0 
</math>

<math > \big(K^{-1}_k \big)_{11} = H_0 + U_k M^{-1}_k U^T_k, \quad U_k = \begin{bmatrix} A^T & S_k & Z_k \end{bmatrix}, \quad  M_k =
\left[\begin{smallmatrix} - AA^T / \gamma_k &  \\  & G_k \end{smallmatrix} \right], \quad  
G_k =  \left[\begin{smallmatrix} R^{-T}_k(D_k+Y^T_k H_0 Y_k) R^{-1}_k & -H_0 R^{-T}_k \\ -H_0R^{-1}_k & 0 \end{smallmatrix} \right]^{-1} </math>

== Limited Memory ==

[[File:Lmupdates fit.gif|thumb|upright=1.|Pattern in a limited-memory updating strategy. With a memory 
parameter of <math>m=7</math>, the first <math> k \le m </math> iterations fill the matrix 
(e.g., an upper triangular for the compact representation, <math>R_k = \text{triu}(S^T_kY_k)</math>). For <math> k > m </math> the limited-memory
techniques discards the oldest information and add a new column to the end.]]

<!-- [[File:Lmupdates fit.gif|thumb|Limited-memory update pattern for a upper triangular matrix]] -->

The most common use of the compact representations is for the [[Limited-memory BFGS|limited-memory]] setting where <math> m \ll n </math> denotes the memory parameter,
with typical values around <math>m \in [5,12]</math> (see e.g.,<ref name="rcr" /><ref name="compact"/>). Then, instead
of storing the history of all vectors one limits this to the <math>m</math> most recent vectors <math> \{ (s_i, y_i \}_{i=k-m}^{k-1} </math> and possibly <math> \{ v_i \}_{i=k-m}^{k-1} </math> or <math> \{ c_i \}_{i=k-m}^{k-1} </math>.
Further, typically the initialization is chosen as an adaptive multiple of the identity <math> H^{(0)}_k = \gamma_k I  </math>,
with <math>\gamma_k = y^T_{k-1} s_{k-1} / y^T_{k-1} y_{k-1} </math> and <math> B^{(0)}_k = \frac{1}{\gamma_k} I  </math>. Limited-memory methods are frequently used for 
large-scale problems with many variables (i.e., <math>n</math> can be large), in which the limited-memory matrices <math> S_k \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times m} </math> 
and <math> Y_k \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times m} </math> (and possibly <math>V_k, C_k </math>) are tall and very skinny:
<math> S_k = \begin{bmatrix} s_{k-l-1} & \ldots & s_{k-1} \end{bmatrix}  </math> and <math> Y_k = \begin{bmatrix} y_{k-l-1} & \ldots & y_{k-1} \end{bmatrix}  </math>.

==Implementations==

Open source implementations include:

* [[ACM Transactions on Mathematical Software|ACM TOMS]] algorithm 1030 implements a L-SR1 solver<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://calgo.acm.org|title=Collected Algorithms of the ACM |website=calgo.acm.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://calgo.acm.org/1030.zip|title=TOMS Alg. 1030|website=calgo.acm.org/1030.zip}}</ref>
* [[R (programming language)|R]]'s <code>optim</code> general-purpose optimizer routine uses the L-BFGS-B method.
* [[SciPy]]'s optimization module's minimize method also includes an option to use L-BFGS-B.
* [[IPOPT]] with first order information

Non open source implementations include:
* [[Artelys Knitro]] [[nonlinear programming]] (NLP) solvers use compact quasi-Newton matrices <ref name="knitro" />
* [[Limited-memory BFGS|L-BFGS-B]] (ACM TOMS algorithm 778)<ref name="algo778">{{cite journal|last1=Zhu|doi=10.1145/279232.279236|first1=C.|last2=Byrd|first2=Richard H.|last3=Lu|first3=Peihuang|last4=Nocedal|first4=Jorge |title=L-BFGS-B: Algorithm 778: L-BFGS-B, FORTRAN routines for large scale bound constrained optimization |year=1997|journal= ACM Transactions on Mathematical Software|volume= 23|issue= 4|pages= 550–560|s2cid=207228122|doi-access=free}}</ref>
